sources.title: Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (Gelman, Hill)
findings: Log transforms for positive right-skewed outcomes; multilevel models partially pool small groups toward the overall mean.
Simulation from the fitted model carries parameter uncertainty into predictions.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Regression and Other Stories (Gelman, Hill, Vehtari)
findings: Bayesian regression with weakly informative default priors; posterior predictive simulation for forecasts instead of plug-in point predictions.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Prior Choice Recommendations (Stan wiki)
findings: Generic weakly informative normal(0, 1) on parameters after scaling; the prior depends on the parameterization.
Half-normal, half-t or half-Cauchy for hierarchical scales; avoid hard bounds unless real.
Student-t with 3 to 7 degrees of freedom is more robust than normal for logistic regression coefficients.
sources.limits: Wiki page, read in this session; living document without a fixed date.

sources.title: Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method (Duan)
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Statistical Association 78(383)
findings: The mean of a log-scale model is not exp of the mean log; the smearing estimate multiplies by the average of exp(residuals) without assuming normal errors.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: An Introduction to the Bootstrap (Efron, Tibshirani)
findings: Percentile and BCa bootstrap intervals; BCa corrects for bias and skewness. That a large gap between them at small n argues for a model-based interval is this Skill's heuristic, not a finding of the book.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory (Kleinrock)
findings: M/M/c and the Erlang C waiting probability; exponential service and Poisson arrivals are assumptions, so bursty arrivals and skewed durations need simulation, with Erlang C as a cross-check.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Estimating log models: to transform or not to transform? (Manning, Mullahy)
findings: Retransformation bias in log-cost models matters when residuals are heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed; check alternatives before trusting exp(sigma^2/2).
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models (Gelman)
findings: Inverse-Gamma(epsilon, epsilon) priors on hierarchical variances cause serious problems; half-t priors are recommended when the number of groups is small.
sources.limits: Abstract and secondary summaries read in this session through a search; full text not re-read.

sources.title: Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models, 2nd edition (Carroll, Ruppert, Stefanski, Crainiceanu)
findings: A covariate or outcome measured with known-direction error can be handled by drawing the error inside the Bayesian fit, so its uncertainty reaches the posterior.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Estimation of relationships for limited dependent variables (Tobin)
findings: Censored regression treats values known only as a bound (for example cost to date of open items) without discarding them.
sources.limits: Bibliographic data and findings as commonly cited; not re-read in this session.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Prediction intervals
findings: Point forecasts can be of almost no value without the accompanying prediction intervals.
Bootstrapped intervals from resampled residuals need no normality assumption and can be asymmetric.
sources.limits: Read in this session; online edition is updated continuously.
sources.revisit: A 4th edition or a rewrite of the section.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Some simple forecasting methods
findings: The mean, naive (last value), seasonal naive (last value of the same season), and drift (average change extended) methods serve as benchmarks.
A new method is worth using only if it beats these benchmarks.
sources.limits: Online edition, updated continuously; read in this session.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Residual diagnostics
findings: Residuals must be uncorrelated with zero mean: leftover correlation means unused information, a nonzero mean means biased forecasts.
Constant variance and normal residuals are useful for intervals but not required; check with a residual time plot, histogram, ACF plot and a portmanteau test (Box-Pierce, Ljung-Box).
sources.limits: Online edition, updated continuously; read in this session.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Evaluating point forecast accuracy and distributional forecast accuracy
findings: Accuracy is judged on a held-out test set (about 20 percent, at least as long as the forecast horizon), not on training residuals, which look better than true forecast errors.
MAE and RMSE are scale-dependent; MAPE is undefined at zero and extreme near zero; MASE scales by the in-sample naive error, below 1 beats the benchmark.

Quantile score (pinball loss), Winkler score for intervals and CRPS (average quantile score over all probabilities) score distributional forecasts; an 80 percent interval should hold the actual about 80 percent of the time.
sources.limits: Online edition, updated continuously; read in this session. The page defines no empirical coverage metric; coverage is stated as the interval's intent.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Time series cross-validation
findings: Evaluates on many test sets, each trained only on earlier observations (a rolling forecasting origin), and averages the accuracy.
A single train/test split gives only one accuracy assessment.
sources.limits: Online edition, updated continuously; read in this session.

sources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), section Transformations and adjustments
findings: Naively back-transforming a forecast usually gives the median, not the mean; a bias adjustment recovers the mean, which matters when forecasts are summed.
Prediction intervals are back-transformed endpoint by endpoint, keeping coverage but becoming asymmetric.
sources.limits: Online edition, updated continuously; read in this session.

sources.title: Value Measurements of Intangibles (Hubbard Decision Research)
findings: Measurement inversion: the more important something is to a decision, the less it tends to be understood and measured.
Intangibles often look unmeasurable only because they are not clearly defined; reduced uncertainty raises the chance of a good decision.
sources.limits: Vendor page; says nothing on calibrated estimates.

sources.title: Applied Information Economics (Hubbard Decision Research)
findings: Applied Information Economics compensates for the natural overconfidence and inconsistency of managers.
Every model variable has an information value that points to the variables worth measuring.
sources.limits: Vendor page; no formulas, no mention of 90 percent intervals or the Rule of Five (page for those not found: calibrated-estimates and rule-of-five returned 404).
